**WASHINGTON —** Sen. Barack Obama has secured enough delegates to claim the 2008 Democratic presidential nomination, making him the first Black candidate to lead a major party ticket in U.S. history and setting up a general election battle with Republican Sen. John McCain.

Obama crossed the delegate threshold Tuesday night after the final Democratic contests in Montana and South Dakota, ending a historic and often bruising primary fight against Sen. Hillary Clinton that stretched through all 50 states and captivated Democratic voters for months.

Speaking to supporters in St. Paul, Minnesota — the city where Republicans will hold their convention later this year — Obama cast his victory as a turning point.

“Tonight, we mark the end of one historic journey with the beginning of another,” Obama said, praising Clinton and calling for party unity as Democrats turn toward the November election.

Clinton, who won South Dakota while Obama was projected to win Montana, did not formally concede Tuesday night. Speaking in New York, she congratulated Obama on his campaign but stopped short of ending her own, telling supporters she would consult with party leaders and backers about the next steps.

“This has been a long campaign, and I will be making no decisions tonight,” Clinton said, while emphasizing that she would work to ensure a Democrat wins the White House in November.

Her remarks immediately fueled speculation about whether she might seek — or be offered — the vice presidential slot on an Obama ticket. Clinton allies have argued that her support among women, working-class voters and key swing-state Democrats could help strengthen the party in the general election. Obama aides, however, have said any decision about a running mate will come later and will be made through a careful vetting process.

The Obama-Clinton contest, one of the closest nomination fights in modern Democratic history, exposed divisions within the party but also produced record turnout and a massive expansion of Democratic voter rolls. Obama built his advantage through caucus wins, strong performances in smaller states and a commanding lead among pledged delegates, while Clinton remained competitive by winning several large states and appealing to late-deciding voters.

McCain, the presumptive Republican nominee, moved quickly to frame the general election as a choice between experience and judgment. In remarks Tuesday night, he congratulated Obama on his achievement but criticized his positions on foreign policy, taxes and government spending.

The Arizona senator’s campaign argued that Obama is too liberal and too inexperienced to be commander in chief, particularly during wartime. Obama, in turn, accused McCain of offering a continuation of President George W. Bush’s policies, especially on Iraq and the economy.

With the Democratic nomination effectively settled, both campaigns are expected to pivot immediately to battleground states, including Ohio, Pennsylvania, Florida, Michigan, Virginia and Colorado. Obama’s next challenge will be uniting Clinton’s supporters behind his candidacy while preparing for a general election fight against a Republican opponent with a long national profile and a reputation for appealing to independents.

The Democratic National Convention is set for August in Denver, where Obama is expected to formally accept the nomination.

# Obama Claims Democratic Nomination as Clinton Stops Short of Conceding

**ST. PAUL, Minnesota —** Sen. Barack Obama effectively secured the Democratic presidential nomination Tuesday night, marking a historic breakthrough as the first Black candidate to become the presumptive nominee of a major U.S. political party.

Speaking to a packed crowd at the Xcel Energy Center in St. Paul — the same arena where Republicans planned to hold their national convention later that year — Obama framed the moment as the closing of one chapter and the beginning of a general-election fight against Sen. John McCain.

“Because of you, tonight I can stand here and say that I will be the Democratic nominee for president of the United States,” Obama told supporters, drawing thunderous applause.

Obama praised Sen. Hillary Clinton, his rival through a long and often bitter primary campaign, calling her a trailblazer who had inspired millions of voters. He said the Democratic Party would need Clinton’s supporters in the fall and emphasized themes of unity after months of state-by-state contests.

The Illinois senator used the speech to pivot toward McCain, arguing that the Arizona Republican represented a continuation of President George W. Bush’s policies on Iraq, the economy and health care. Obama sought to cast the general election as a choice between “change” and the status quo, a message that had fueled his campaign from its earliest days.

## Clinton Addresses Supporters in New York

Earlier in the evening, Clinton appeared before supporters in New York and acknowledged the strength of her campaign, but she did not formally concede the race.

“This has been a long campaign, and I will be making no decisions tonight,” Clinton said, while thanking voters, donors, volunteers and staff who had sustained her bid through the final primaries.

The New York senator stressed the scale of her support, noting that millions had voted for her and that her candidacy had broken barriers for women in American politics. She said she would consult with party leaders and supporters about the path forward.

Clinton’s remarks left open questions about when and how she would exit the race, even as Obama’s delegate advantage had become decisive. Her campaign had argued for months that she was better positioned to win key swing states against McCain, while Obama’s team pointed to his lead in pledged delegates, states won and overall momentum.

## Talk Turns to a Unity Ticket

With the nomination fight nearing its end, attention quickly shifted to whether Obama might ask Clinton to be his running mate.

A possible Obama-Clinton ticket was already a subject of intense speculation among Democrats. Supporters of the idea argued that Clinton could help unify the party, bring in working-class voters and women who had backed her strongly, and add experience to the ticket.

But others warned that combining the two campaigns could create complications. The primary contest had exposed sharp tensions between the Obama and Clinton camps, and questions remained about how former President Bill Clinton would fit into a general-election campaign. Some Obama allies also argued that he should choose a running mate who reinforced his message of change rather than one tied to the political battles of the 1990s.

Clinton did not publicly ask to be considered for vice president Tuesday night, but her campaign’s emphasis on her vote totals and influence within the party underscored that she remained a major force.

## A Historic Primary Season Ends

The 2008 Democratic race stretched across five months of primaries and caucuses and transformed both candidates into symbols of political change: Obama as a first-term senator who energized young voters and African Americans, and Clinton as the first woman to come closer than any before her to a major-party presidential nomination.

Obama’s victory rested on early wins in Iowa and other caucus states, strong support from Black voters, and a disciplined delegate strategy. Clinton rebounded repeatedly in large states such as Ohio, Pennsylvania and Texas, but was unable to erase Obama’s delegate lead.

Now, Obama faces the task of bringing together a divided Democratic Party while preparing for a general election against McCain, a decorated Vietnam War veteran and longtime senator.

In St. Paul, Obama made clear that he saw the night not only as a personal milestone, but as a turning point.

“The journey will be difficult,” he told supporters. “The road will be long. But we are ready.”

Several Clinton supporters chanted “Denver! Denver!” — a reference to the Democratic National Convention — while others shouted “Yes, she will!” when the possibility of continuing was raised.

Obama’s victory capped a campaign that began with him as an underdog against Clinton, the early Democratic front-runner and former first lady. His message of change, opposition to the Iraq war, fundraising operation and strength in caucus states helped him build a delegate lead Clinton could not overcome, despite her victories in several large states late in the race.

With the Democratic contest effectively settled, the general election matchup between Obama and Sen. John McCain began immediately.

McCain, the presumptive Republican nominee, addressed supporters Tuesday night in New Orleans and sought to cast Obama as inexperienced and too liberal, while also congratulating him on his achievement.

“Senator Obama has achieved a great thing, for himself and for his country,” McCain said. “I congratulate him.”

But McCain quickly pivoted to the fall campaign, arguing that Obama’s promise of change would mean higher taxes and expanded government.

“That’s not change we can believe in,” McCain said.

Obama, in turn, drew a sharp contrast with McCain, linking the Arizona senator to President Bush’s policies on Iraq, the economy and health care.

“There are many words to describe John McCain’s attempt to pass off his embrace of George Bush’s policies as bipartisan and new,” Obama said. “But ‘change’ is not one of them.”

The historic nature of Obama’s nomination was not lost on supporters gathered in St. Paul. Many waved American flags and signs reading “Change We Can Believe In,” while others wiped away tears as Obama spoke.

The nomination comes 45 years after the height of the civil rights movement and places Obama, the son of a Kenyan father and a mother from Kansas, at the center of a presidential campaign that will test the nation’s political and racial boundaries.

Obama closed his speech by urging Democrats to unite after the bruising primary fight.

“The journey will be difficult. The road will be long,” he said. “I face this challenge with profound humility and knowledge of my own limitations. But I also face it with limitless faith in the capacity of the American people.”
